archetype.name: Pocket Passer (veteran spot starter)
archetype.definition: A big, 6-foot-5 pocket thrower who now plays it safe with modest aggression, keeps the ball away from defenders, and gives back yards by taking sacks when the first read isn't there.

report.headline: Steady, turnover-free fill-in whose sack habit caps what a good defense covers
report.take:
Wentz is Minnesota's QB2, and his 2026 is two games of relief work. He took 83% of the snaps in Week 1 after Kyler Murray started, then started and won 9-3 at Chicago. Murray has started the two games since. This is a 48-dropback sample from a backup on a team built around the league's best defense: first in EPA, pass EPA, success rate, hit rate and sack rate. The offense is 28th in EPA, dead last in success rate, and passes 5 points less than situation predicts. His job in that ecosystem is not to lose games, and he did that well. He threw no interceptions, lost no fumbles, and the team went 2-0.

The production is less even than the 0.122 EPA per dropback suggests. Week 1 against Green Bay, now a 26th-ranked defense, produced 5.0 passing EPA and three touchdowns on 19 attempts. Week 2 against Chicago, now 5th, produced 0.5 EPA and 143 yards. Much of the season's value sits in a handful of plays: three deep attempts worth 1.7 EPA apiece, two no-huddle snaps at 3.5 each, and one touchdown while up 9+. In one-score game states his EPA is exactly 0. Underneath that, his accuracy has been poor. His CPOE of -7.79 ranks 37th of 42, his bad-throw rate of 20.5% is at the bottom of the charted group, and he was 38.5% on throws to the left.

The sacks are the real issue, and they aren't new. He was pressured on only 20% of dropbacks, a middle-of-the-pack rate, but two-thirds of those pressures became sacks. That is the main reason his sack rate of 13.3% ranks last of 42. His time to throw of 2.61 isn't long, so this isn't a scrambler trading sacks for creation. He had two scrambles for 5 yards and no first downs. His pressure-to-sack rates of .336 in 2020, .371 in 2022 and .396 last year in Minnesota say this is who he has become: when the picture muddies, he eats it rather than throwing it away or escaping.

The good part also holds up across seasons. When he works the middle, where Justin Jefferson and T.J. Hockenson live, he is efficient: 0.894 EPA and 75% completions on 12 middle throws, with both targets near 0.9 EPA per target. On a team whose defense wins most weeks, a careful backup who can hit the seams is a reasonable insurance policy. He is not a starter who lifts the offense.

strengths.title: Ball security in a defense-first team
strengths.body: He has no interceptions and no lost fumbles across 48 dropbacks. His one turnover-worthy play was a fumble, not a throw. Last year's 5 INTs in 5 games say the zero will rise. Still, his low 12.8% aggressiveness reflects a conscious conservatism that fits an offense leaning on the No. 1 defense.

strengths.title: Middle-of-field efficiency with top targets
strengths.body: Throws between the numbers have been his best work, and Jefferson and Hockenson turned their combined 22 targets into roughly 0.9 EPA each. That comes from easy, defined reads to the two best players in the offense. It is real but depends on those two being on the field.

strengths.title: Composure in close fourth quarters
strengths.body: In close fourth quarters he was successful on 70% of 10 plays, completing 77.8% of his throws. On third down he completed 76.5% with a positive CPOE. These are tiny samples, but they match a veteran who doesn't panic when the game tightens.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: Only 20% of his dropbacks saw pressure, but 66.7% of those ended in sacks. That drove a sack rate that ranks last among 42 qualifiers. It isn't the cost of play extension: he barely scrambles and holds the ball a normal 2.61 seconds. His pressure-to-sack rate has sat near .34 to .40 in recent full seasons, so expect it to last.

concerns.title: Accuracy below expectation everywhere
concerns.body: Outside the middle he has been poor. He sits at -15.9 CPOE behind the line, -12.2 on short throws and 38.5% completions to the left. One in five throws was charted as bad. His career CPOE has been negative in most seasons, so this is closer to his baseline than to noise.

concerns.title: EPA propped up by few plays
concerns.body: Three deep throws, two no-huddle snaps and one long touchdown while ahead carry an outsized share of his positive EPA. In one-score game states he is at exactly 0.00 EPA per play. The Week 1 versus Week 2 split against a weak and a strong defense shows the same thing.

trend.note: He posted a 5.0-EPA relief outing against a soft Green Bay defense, then a grind-it-out 0.5-EPA start in a 9-3 win at Chicago. Murray has started both games since, so Wentz's arc is now on hold as QB2.

nextGame.headline: Soft Saints defense, but he's QB2 without Jefferson
nextGame.body:
If Wentz plays at New Orleans, the matchup is about as kind as it gets. The Saints rank 30th in defensive EPA, 27th against the pass, 25th on deep throws and 25th on short throws. Their 5.8% sack rate is middle of the pack, which matters for a quarterback whose biggest leak is sacks. The catch is that he is listed as QB2 behind Murray, and nothing in the dossier suggests Murray is unavailable. His realistic expectation is zero snaps unless something changes in-game.

Availability cuts both ways. Minnesota is without Justin Jefferson (ankle), its most efficient target for Wentz. Josh Oliver is on IR, guard Donovan Jackson is out after meniscus surgery, and left tackle Christian Darrisaw is questionable in concussion protocol. A patched-up line in front of a quarterback who converts pressure to sacks at 66.7% is a real worry. On the other side, New Orleans is missing linebacker Kaden Elliss (a 100%-snap player) and edge Carl Granderson. Defensive tackle Davon Godchaux is questionable. That thins a pass rush that was only average to begin with.

keyMatchups.title: Patched Vikings line vs Saints rush
keyMatchups.body: With Jackson out and Darrisaw uncertain, Minnesota's protection weakens. That is exactly where Wentz is most vulnerable. The Saints' missing edge and linebacker offset some of that. Their middling sack rate gives a quarterback who rarely escapes some breathing room.

keyMatchups.title: Middle of the field without Jefferson
keyMatchups.body: Wentz's efficiency lives between the numbers, and Jefferson drew 14 of his targets at 0.931 EPA each. Without Jefferson, Hockenson becomes the middle-of-field read. Addison has been negative EPA per target with Wentz.

keyMatchups.title: Top defense vs short spread
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota's defense ranks first in EPA and success rate. New Orleans' ranks 30th in EPA and last in success rate and rush EPA. A 1.5-point spread barely prices that gap, even with the Vikings' offensive injuries.

nextGame.watch: Whether Murray is active and healthy. Wentz's game only exists if he isn't.

restOfSeason.body:
As QB2, Wentz's season is a series of possible spot appearances. When he plays, expect roughly what he has been for years: competent and fairly careful with the ball, not accurate, and a sack magnet behind any line under strain. The zero interceptions will regress, since he threw 5 in 5 games last year. The deep-ball and no-huddle EPA spikes won't repeat at that rate. The high sack rate is sticky and may get worse with Jackson out and Darrisaw uncertain.

If he makes starts, the context helps him win more than it helps his stat line. A run-leaning offense and the league's top defense mean modest volume. Think 20 to 30 attempts in short, defensive games. Games like the Week 2 win at Chicago are more typical of what he'd offer than Week 1's three-touchdown relief outing.
swingFactors: Murray's health and the depth chart
Darrisaw's return and the interior line after Jackson's injury

bets.reason: The Vikings have the league's No. 1 defense by EPA, success rate and sack rate, facing a Saints defense ranked 30th in EPA and 32nd in success rate. A short spread underprices that gap, though Jefferson's absence and a banged-up line keep this a lean rather than a strong play.

Minnesota's offense is last in success rate and passes 5 points under expectation, and it is now without Jefferson and Jackson. Its top-ranked defense faces a middling Saints offense. The Saints' poor run defense invites a clock-heavy Vikings plan, which also favors the under.

confidence.note: Two games and 48 dropbacks, as a backup unlikely to play next week; career trends do most of the work.
